ai_summary:
Great Britain is currently generating 11.5 GW of wind power, with Scotland delivering an estimated 4.3 GW, representing 42.6% of installed Scottish wind capacity. This robust renewable output has driven Scottish carbon intensity down to 0 gCO2/kWh, standing in sharp contrast to 62 gCO2/kWh GB-wide. However, severe north-to-south transmission bottlenecks prevent this clean power from reaching major demand centres. As a result, Scottish generation curtailed so far today has reached 13.8 GWh, incurring Balancing Mechanism constraint payments of about £761,214. 

To replace this locked-in generation and meet demand south of the border, an estimated 2,613,507 m³ of gas was burned elsewhere, releasing an avoidable 4,814 tonnes of CO2 into the atmosphere. Annualising today's expenditure highlights a chronic grid efficiency challenge, representing an estimated total yearly curtailment cost of £278 million. Distributed across national electricity consumption through system balancing charges, this constraint burden adds an estimated £1/MWh to everybody's invoice in the UK. Without expedited investment in transmission infrastructure between Scotland and England, consumers will continue to fund payments to turn off low-cost zero-carbon generators while simultaneously paying fossil plants to replace them.
